title: Sleep warm
summary: Insulate from the ground first, keep your bag or blankets dry and fluffed, eat a snack and go to the bathroom before bed, and add a wrapped bottle of warm water. Never sleep with a fuel-burning heater, stove, lantern or engine running in a tent, vehicle or any room where people are sleeping.

blocks.warn: Never use a charcoal grill, lantern or portable camping stove inside a tent or snow shelter, and never use fuel-burning heaters or lanterns while sleeping in one. Carbon monoxide kills people every year this way (Shelter, Priorities).

list: Indoors: never run an unvented fuel-burning appliance in any room where people are sleeping (CPSC). Turn heaters off when you go to bed (US Fire Administration). See Carbon monoxide and Kerosene and propane heaters.
In a vehicle: never run the engine while people are sleeping (Carbon monoxide protocol). Run it only while someone is awake, and take turns sleeping (Red Cross). See Winter storms.
Wood stove or fireplace overnight: follow its topic.
Keep battery carbon monoxide alarms near where people sleep (Carbon monoxide).

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

blocks.p: At rest you can lose as much as 80 percent of your body heat to the ground (Shelter). Insulate under you before you add anything on top.

list: Don’t sleep directly on the ground: use a sleeping pad. Put a tarp or poncho on the ground under the pad and bag (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).

No pad: build a bed from foam rubber from vehicle seats, or boughs, leaves or dry moss (Army FM 21-76-1). A bed of dry leaves, grass or boughs should be at least 12 inches (30 cm) thick, because it packs down when you lie on it (Shelter).

On snow, remove snow down toward ground level or pack it down, so you have a comfortable shelf to sleep on (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research). In a snow trench or cave, sleep on a platform higher than the entrance (Shelter).
Use a waterproof cover (bivy) over the sleeping bag if there is rain or snow (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).
Shake the sleeping bag out and fluff it up before and after use (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research), especially at the foot (Army FM 21-76-1).

Keep it dry: carry it in a waterproof bag (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research), and air and dry it every day to remove body moisture (Army FM 21-76-1). Open it wide or turn it inside out so sun and wind can dry it, and remove any frost that builds up overnight (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).

Adults: sleep in dry wool or synthetic clothing, socks and a hat, not cotton. Don’t overdress: you shouldn’t sweat (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research). Babies sleep by different rules: see Stay warm when the heat is out.
If there is room, put dry boots and clothes inside the bag with you (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).
Once you are in bed, try not to get out of the bag (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).
Not enough bag: add dry grass, leaves or dry moss (Army FM 21-76-1).

blocks.p: Indoors with no heat, use blankets and sleeping bags, with lots of covers (Stay warm when the heat is out).

list: Eat plenty through the day, with warm meals and warm sugary drinks (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research). Your body needs fuel to make heat (Priorities).
Have an easy-to-digest or warm snack just before you get into the bag: it can help you stay warmer longer while you sleep (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).
Go to the bathroom (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).
Warm up with a few exercises, but don’t break a sweat (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research).

If you can heat water, fill a bottle that closes tightly with warmed water and put it in the bag (Walter Reed Army Institute of Research). Wrap it in cloth: never put a hot water bottle directly on the skin (Hypothermia protocol).

blocks.p: Keep drinking through the day: cold weather dulls your thirst (Water in winter).

list: Huddle with other people for warmth (CDC, said of people stranded in a car).
At home with no heat, bed with other family members and lots of covers is the warmest place, but not for babies (Stay warm when the heat is out).

blocks.warn: Babies: “Infants less than one year old should never sleep in a cold room because they lose body heat more easily than adults” (CDC). The family bed is not for babies: follow Babies: warm and safe asleep in Stay warm when the heat is out.

blocks.label: Stay warm when the heat is out

blocks.p: Someone who is cold and confused, drowsy, mumbling or fumbling needs more than a better bed: open the Hypothermia protocol.
